title: Suppressing Cavity Frequency Noise Using a Kerr Nonlinearity
authors: J. P. van Soest, S. Meilof, G. L. Bhai, M. Villiers, C. A. Potts, G. A. Steele
abstract: Resonance-frequency fluctuations can limit the sensitivity and stability of superconducting microwave cavities used for qubit readout, optomechanical displacement sensing, and magnetic flux detection. Here, we demonstrate the suppression of resonance-frequency fluctuations by locking a noisy nonlinear superconducting microwave cavity to a strong pump tone. The Kerr nonlinearity of this system, whereby the resonance frequency depends on the intracavity field amplitude, gives rise to an intrinsic feedback mechanism that enables passive stabilization without active external feedback. Using two-tone spectroscopy, we experimentally characterize the intrinsic nonlinear feedback mechanism and investigate its temporal stability through Allan deviation analysis. The frequency fluctuations of the locked cavity mode are reduced by nearly two orders of magnitude, reaching the $1/f$ noise floor, without continuous frequency tracking or active control. Kerr locking provides a general approach for self-stabilizing nonlinear microwave resonators by suppressing low-frequency cavity noise while preserving sensitivity to signals outside the locking bandwidth. This approach may benefit a broad range of systems, including SQUID-based resonators, optomechanical devices, and parametric amplifiers.
summary: The authors demonstrate that by exploiting the Kerr nonlinearity inherent in superconducting microwave cavities, they can passively stabilize resonance frequency fluctuations. This 'Kerr locking' technique suppresses noise by two orders of magnitude without requiring active feedback loops. The method offers a general approach for stabilizing various nonlinear resonators used across quantum sensing and computing platforms.
main_problem: Resonance-frequency fluctuations limit the sensitivity of superconducting microwave cavities used for various quantum measurements.
main_result: The intrinsic Kerr nonlinearity provides a passive feedback mechanism that suppresses cavity frequency noise by nearly two orders of magnitude, reaching the $1/f$ noise floor without active control.
method: Two-tone spectroscopy and Allan deviation analysis were used to experimentally characterize the nonlinear feedback and measure temporal stability.
model_or_system: The system is a superconducting microwave cavity incorporating a flux-tunable transmon qubit, which induces a Kerr nonlinearity ($K_c$). The stabilization mechanism involves locking the noisy cavity mode to a strong pump tone.
key_observables: Frequency fluctuations ($\sigma_{std}$), Allan deviation ($\sigma_f(	au)$), and the transfer function $T(\omega_m)$.
important_parameters: Pump detuning ($\Delta_p$), Kerr nonlinearity coefficient ($K_c$), cavity linewidth ($\kappa$).
main_assumptions: The stabilization relies on operating in a regime where the intrinsic nonlinear feedback dominates over external noise sources.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spectroscopy response before and after locking, showing frequency stabilization; time dynamics plots compare standard deviations (MHz to kHz); and Allan deviation plots quantify the noise floor reduction.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the problem of cavity noise limitation. It then details the Kerr-locking mechanism using theoretical modeling (Bogoliubov modes) and experimental characterization via two-tone spectroscopy, culminating in quantitative analysis of noise suppression using Allan deviation.
why_interesting: This work demonstrates a purely nonlinear, passive method for stabilizing high-quality microwave resonators, which is crucial for building sensitive quantum sensors and improving readout fidelity in superconducting quantum circuits.
